topics.title: The Roman Republic
topics.summary: Rome's period of elected, shared government before the rise of the emperors.

lessons.title: How the Republic Was Governed

sections.heading: Two consuls instead of a king
sections.body:
Imagine waking up in a city that has just thrown out its king. What would you put in his place? By the end of the Republic, Romans generally accepted a traditional story: Rome had been ruled by seven kings, and in 509 BCE the last of them, Lucius Tarquinius Superbus, was overthrown. Rather than crown someone new, the Romans replaced kingship with two magistrates called consuls, elected every year. Two leaders instead of one, and only for a year: that design tells you what Romans feared most.

To see how the system worked from the inside, follow one real career through it. Marcus Tullius Cicero was born in 106 BCE in Arpinum, a town in Latium outside Rome. He was what Romans called a “new man,” someone without noble ancestry. Nobody handed Cicero a place at the top. He had to climb, office by office and election by election, and his path will take you through the machinery of the Republic.

Start with the office Cicero eventually reached. The two consuls were, above all, generals whose task was to lead Rome’s armies in war. In a military emergency, when a single commander seemed necessary, Rome could appoint a dictator in place of the consuls. Even then there was a limit: a dictator could not hold supreme military command for longer than six months. In this system, even the exception came with an expiration date.

sections.heading: Climbing the ladder of offices
sections.body:
Roman politicians of senatorial rank followed a set sequence of public offices known as the cursus honorum, the “course of honors.” Over time, laws regulated the ladder. Holding the same magistracy a second time was prohibited, and the praetorship became a requirement for anyone seeking the consulship. Ambition was allowed, but it had to move in order.

Cicero’s career follows that path. After making his name as a lawyer, he began his public career in 75 BCE as quaestor, an office of financial administration, in western Sicily. In 66 BCE he served as praetor, a judicial office of great power at the time. He was then elected consul for 63 BCE, helped by conservative senators who feared the revolutionary ideas of his rival, Catiline. A man without noble ancestry had reached the Republic’s highest regular office.

Who did the electing? Romans voted in popular assemblies. The centuriate assembly, military in nature, voted on war and peace and elected the magistrates who held imperium, or military power, including consuls and praetors. The tribal assembly was a civilian body that elected magistrates without imperium and did most of the legislating. So when Cicero ran for praetor and then consul, he was asking the centuriate assembly for its votes.

sections.heading: Balanced, or tilted toward the few?
sections.body:
Then there was the Senate, which may already have advised the kings. Under the Republic it advised both the magistrates and the Roman people. In theory the people were sovereign and the Senate only offered advice, but in practice it wielded enormous power because of the collective prestige of its members. It also controlled the treasury: the Greek historian Polybius noted that, apart from payments to the consuls, quaestors could not spend public money without a decree of the Senate. Cicero the quaestor would have worked inside exactly that rule.

Citizens were also divided into patricians, members of privileged families, and plebeians, the general citizenry. Plebeians were originally excluded from the Senate and from almost all public offices. In a long campaign called the Conflict of the Orders, which lasted until 287 BCE, they withdrew from the state on several occasions to force concessions, elected their own officials called tribunes, and won the inviolability of those tribunes. Polybius observed that if a single tribune interposed, the Senate could not reach a final decision on a matter or even meet.

Polybius admired the result. He argued that the consuls made Rome look monarchical, the Senate aristocratic, and the people democratic, so that even a Roman could not say which the constitution was. But look closely at the voting. In the centuriate assembly, citizens were grouped by wealth, voting started with the wealthier groups, and their votes outweighed those of the poorer. Cicero’s story cuts both ways: a new man could rise, yet the dominant circle of conservative senators never fully accepted him. Whether the Republic was a balance or a system tilted toward the wealthy is a question worth keeping open.

keyFacts: By Roman tradition, the Republic began in 509 BCE, when the last king was overthrown.
Two consuls were elected every year; a dictator could hold supreme command for no more than six months.
The cursus honorum was a fixed sequence of offices, and the praetorship became a requirement for the consulship.
Cicero, a “new man,” was quaestor in 75 BCE, praetor in 66 BCE, and consul in 63 BCE.
In the centuriate assembly, the wealthier groups voted first and their votes outweighed those of the poorer.

quiz.question: Rome faces a sudden military emergency and wants a single commander in charge. What could it do under the Republic?
options: Crown a new king for life.
Appoint a dictator, whose supreme command could last no more than six months.
Let the Senate choose one consul for ten years.
Hand command of the army to the tribunes of the plebs.
quiz.explanation: In military emergencies Rome could appoint a dictator in place of the consuls, but only for up to six months.

quiz.question: An ambitious Roman wants to run for consul next year but has never served as praetor. What stands in his way?
options: Consuls were appointed by the outgoing dictator.
Only former quaestors of Sicily could become consul.
The praetorship had become a requirement for the consulship.
The consulship could be held only by members of the Senate’s oldest families.
quiz.explanation: Laws regulating the cursus honorum made the praetorship a prerequisite for the consulship.

quiz.question: What does Cicero’s path from quaestor to consul suggest about Roman politics?
options: A man without noble ancestry could rise by winning elections, though the elite never fully accepted him.
Offices were inherited from father to son.
Consuls were chosen by drawing lots.
Only patricians could hold any office at all.
quiz.explanation: Cicero was a “new man” who climbed office by office to the consulship, yet the dominant circle of conservative senators never fully accepted him.

quiz.question: The Senate is about to decide a matter when a tribune of the plebs interposes. According to Polybius, what happens?
options: The matter automatically becomes law.
The tribune immediately becomes consul.
The consuls remove the tribune from office.
The Senate cannot reach a final decision on the matter.
quiz.explanation: Polybius wrote that if a single tribune interposed, the Senate could not decide finally about any matter, or even meet.

quiz.question: Poorer citizens greatly outnumber the wealthy in the centuriate assembly. Why might the wealthy still decide an election?
options: Poorer citizens were barred from attending.
Citizens voted in groups by wealth, the wealthier groups voted first, and their votes outweighed the poorer.
The Senate counted the votes in secret.
Only the consuls were allowed to vote.
quiz.explanation: The centuriate assembly grouped citizens by wealth, and the wealthier centuries voted first with votes that outweighed the poorer ones.

quiz.question: A friend says, “The Senate only gave advice, so it had little real power.” What is the best response?
options: That is right; the magistrates usually ignored it.
The Senate was the only body the people elected directly.
In theory it only advised, but its prestige gave it enormous power, and it controlled public spending.
The Senate replaced the consuls after 509 BCE.
quiz.explanation: The Senate’s role was advisory in theory, but its members’ collective prestige gave it great power, and Polybius notes its control of the treasury.

topics.title: The French Revolution
topics.summary: The upheaval of 1789-1799 that overthrew the French monarchy and spread ideas of rights and citizenship.

lessons.title: 1789: The Revolution Begins

sections.heading: A kingdom that couldn’t pay its bills
sections.body:
Picture a government that has been spending far more than it takes in, year after year, and covering the gap by borrowing. That was the French monarchy in the 1780s, partly because of the long, costly wars of the eighteenth century. Then the borrowing dried up. Historians still argue about exactly why, but the result was clear: mounting debt pushed the monarchy toward fundamental financial change.

In 1787 the royal government proposed major reforms to taxation and spending. They met furious resistance from a special Assembly of Notables and from the king’s own law courts, especially the Parlement of Paris. These bodies insisted on an old tradition: the French people had once consented to royal decrees through a representative body called the Estates-General. It had not met since 1614, but many saw it as the only national body with the authority to approve reforms and new taxes. Facing imminent bankruptcy, Louis XVI called it in the fall of 1788.

Now meet the person whose ideas will run through this whole lesson. Emmanuel-Joseph Sieyès was a churchman and constitutional theorist. In January 1789 he wrote a pamphlet called What Is the Third Estate?, arguing that the unprivileged Third Estate, everyone outside the clergy and the nobility, was the French nation itself. In an 1899 English translation, his answer to his own title question is blunt: “Everything; but an everything shackled and oppressed.”

sections.heading: The fight over how to count votes
sections.body:
Here is the problem Sieyès was attacking. Traditionally, the Estates-General had three estates, the clergy, the nobility, and the commons, each with the same number of deputies and a single vote. Under that arrangement the nobility always dominated, because the clerical deputies included a majority of nobles. Leading nobles wanted to keep this “voting by order,” and many commoners reacted angrily. If you were a Third Estate deputy, you could do the math: two votes against one, every time.

The pamphlet made Sieyès immensely popular and ensured his election to the Estates-General, which convened on May 5, 1789. Divisions between noble and commoner deputies only deepened. On June 17, on Sieyès’s motion, the deputies of the Third Estate proclaimed themselves a National Assembly, claiming that they alone represented the nation. It was a radical departure that struck directly at the political basis of the monarchy.

Three days later, on June 20, the deputies found themselves locked out of their usual meeting hall at Versailles. Thinking the king meant to force them to disband, they moved to a nearby indoor tennis court and swore never to separate until a written constitution had been established for France. Louis XVI wavered. He refused to recognize the “National Assembly,” yet he also agreed to become a constitutional monarch, a pattern of ambivalence that would continue.

sections.heading: Paris, the countryside, and a declaration of rights
sections.body:
By mid-July, Paris was tense. The deputies at Versailles had been thwarted by the king, and on July 12 Parisians learned that the popular finance minister Jacques Necker had been dismissed. On July 14 a crowd swarmed the Bastille, a medieval royal fortress looming over the workers’ neighborhoods, and took it. Was this a deliberate political act to protect the deputies from royal interference, or a large-scale bread riot that took on political meaning as events unfolded? Bread prices were rising sharply, and historians still debate the question.

The upheaval spread to the countryside. When peasants heard about the Bastille, rumors also circulated of armed “brigands” coming to burn fields and attack villages. Driven by what became known as the Great Fear, peasants formed armed groups to defend their villages. The National Assembly, feeling pressure to stay ahead of events, responded with the decrees of August 4, announcing the “abolition of feudalism.” They were a first step toward dismantling the old regime’s system of privileges.

On August 26, 1789, the National Assembly approved the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. Its first article states that men are born and remain free and equal in rights, and that social distinctions may be founded only upon the general good. You can hear Sieyès’s argument in it: privilege has to justify itself. On October 5–6, with bread prices at their highest level of the century, a crowd of women marched from Paris to Versailles and forced the royal family back to Paris. Soon afterward Louis consented to sign the Declaration.

keyFacts: The Estates-General had not met since 1614; it convened on May 5, 1789.
Under “voting by order,” each of the three estates had a single vote.
On June 17, 1789, on Sieyès’s motion, the Third Estate proclaimed itself the National Assembly.
Crowds took the Bastille on July 14, 1789.
The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen was approved on August 26, 1789.

quiz.question: Under “voting by order,” the clergy and the nobility support a proposal and the Third Estate opposes it. What happens?
options: The proposal passes, two votes to one.
The proposal fails, because the Third Estate had the most deputies.
The king must break the tie.
Each deputy votes individually, so the outcome is uncertain.
quiz.explanation: Each estate had a single vote, so the two privileged orders could outvote the Third Estate every time.

quiz.question: Sieyès argued that the Third Estate was the whole nation. Which event in 1789 put that idea into action?
options: Louis XVI calling the Estates-General in 1788.
The Third Estate proclaiming itself the National Assembly on June 17.
The Assembly of Notables resisting reform in 1787.
The women’s march to Versailles in October.
quiz.explanation: On Sieyès’s motion, the Third Estate deputies declared that they alone represented the nation and formed the National Assembly.

quiz.question: Imagine you are one of the deputies taking the Tennis Court Oath. What are you promising?
options: To restore voting by order.
To leave Versailles and return home.
Never to separate until France has a written constitution.
To give the king full control of taxation.
quiz.explanation: Locked out of their hall on June 20, the deputies swore never to separate until a written constitution had been established.

quiz.question: A historian notes that bread prices in Paris were rising sharply in July 1789. Which interpretation of the taking of the Bastille does this evidence support?
options: The attack was planned by royal troops.
The Bastille was taken to celebrate the Declaration of Rights.
Nobles organized the crowd to defend voting by order.
The crowd may have begun with a bread riot that took on political meaning as events unfolded.
quiz.explanation: Historians debate whether the crowd acted to protect the deputies or engaged in a traditional bread riot that became political; rising bread prices support the second view.

quiz.question: Peasants hear rumors that “brigands” are coming to burn their crops, and they arm themselves. How did the National Assembly respond to movements like this?
options: With the decrees of August 4, announcing the abolition of feudalism.
By recalling the Assembly of Notables.
By restoring the old voting rules.
By moving the Assembly back to the tennis court.
quiz.explanation: Feeling pressure from the Great Fear in the countryside, the Assembly announced the abolition of feudalism on August 4.

quiz.question: Why did Louis XVI end up calling the Estates-General at all?
options: Because the Third Estate had already declared a republic.
Because bankruptcy loomed and powerful bodies insisted only the Estates-General could approve reforms and new taxes.
Because it met every year by law.
Because Sieyès’s pamphlet ordered him to.
quiz.explanation: Mounting debt and resistance from the Notables and the Parlement, who looked to the Estates-General, forced the king to call it in 1788.

lessons.title: Republic and Terror

sections.heading: From king to citizen
sections.body:
In 1789 Maximilien Robespierre, born in Arras in 1758, was elected to represent the Third Estate of Artois in the Estates-General. From the very beginning he spoke for popular causes, and admirers called him “the Incorruptible.” Keep him in view throughout this lesson. His path shows how a revolution that began by limiting a king ended by executing one, and then turned on its own leaders.

At first, almost no one imagined France without a king. That changed fast. In June 1791 the royal family fled Paris in disguise, but the king was recognized and arrested at Varennes. A majority of the Assembly accepted his weak excuse, fearing that punishing him would destabilize the country. Then came war: in April 1792 the Girondin leaders of the new Legislative Assembly declared war on Austria, and early French defeats panicked Paris.

On August 10, 1792, Parisian militants known as sans-culottes invaded the Tuileries Palace and effectively deposed the king. A new National Convention met in September and, after news of the first great French victory at Valmy, declared France a republic. In December the Convention began Louis’s trial; it voted unanimously to convict him of treason and sentenced him to death. He was executed by guillotine in January 1793 before tens of thousands of onlookers.

sections.heading: Government by Terror
sections.body:
Governing in wartime through a quarrelsome legislature of some 600 members proved nearly impossible. So in the spring of 1793 the Convention handed power to a twelve-member Committee of Public Safety. Pressure was coming from every side: foreign war, a peasant revolt in the Vendée sparked by a call for 300,000 army “volunteers,” and revolts in cities that rejected rule from Paris. On July 27, 1793, Robespierre took his seat on the Committee, and in the following months he came to dominate it.

In early September 1793, pushed by the sans-culottes, the Committee led the Convention into what became known as the Terror. Britannica dates it from September 5, 1793, to July 27, 1794. In practice it meant the organized use of state power to force compliance: revolutionary tribunals tried “suspects” for treason and sent those convicted to the guillotine. The Terror also enforced price controls known as the maximum, and pursued vaguer aims such as ensuring the “virtue” of all citizens.

The scale was enormous. About 300,000 people were arrested, and 17,000 of them were tried and executed. As many as 23,000 more were killed without trial or died in prison. Deputies sent out as “representatives on mission” often became the most zealous enforcers; at Nantes, one ordered thousands of rebels drowned in the Loire. By the end of 1793 even radical Jacobins such as Georges Danton argued that the violence had gone too far.

sections.heading: The fall of the Incorruptible
sections.body:
In June 1794 Robespierre staged the Festival of the Supreme Being, an attempt at a civic religion, with himself in the leading role. Two days later he pushed through the Law of 22 Prairial (June 10, 1794), which put the machinery of the Terror directly under the Committee’s control and made openly political prosecutions easier. He defended it as a way to instill virtue, but many deputies concluded that he wanted to eliminate his opponents and rule alone.

In late July 1794, in the coup known by its revolutionary calendar date, 9 Thermidor, Robespierre and a number of his followers were arrested at the Hôtel de Ville in Paris. He was executed on July 28. Notice the motive: the men who brought him down acted mainly to save themselves from the Terror, not to end it. Only over the following months were the Law of 22 Prairial repealed, the revolutionary tribunals abolished, and the price controls abandoned.

Historians still disagree about what the Terror means. Some argue it grew out of 1789 itself, whether as the necessary sweeping away of the old regime or because the revolutionaries had unknowingly built authoritarianism into their democratic principles. Others see a revolution swept off course by war, revolt, and economic crisis. The revolutionary decade ended with a twist: in November 1799 Sieyès, the author of What Is the Third Estate?, helped arrange the coup that brought General Napoleon Bonaparte to power.

keyFacts: France was declared a republic in September 1792, and Louis XVI was executed in January 1793.
The twelve-member Committee of Public Safety was created in spring 1793; Robespierre joined it in July 1793.
Britannica dates the Reign of Terror from September 5, 1793, to July 27, 1794.
About 17,000 people were tried and executed; as many as 23,000 more died without trial or in prison.
Robespierre was arrested on July 27, 1794, and executed the next day.

quiz.question: In late 1793 a shopkeeper is accused of being an enemy of the Revolution. Which institution would most likely try them?
options: The Estates-General.
The Directory.
A revolutionary tribunal.
The Parlement of Paris.
quiz.explanation: During the Terror, revolutionary tribunals tried “suspects” for treason and sent those convicted to the guillotine.

quiz.question: Why did the Law of 22 Prairial alarm many deputies in June 1794?
options: It abolished the Committee of Public Safety.
It put the Terror under the Committee’s direct control, making political prosecutions easier.
It restored the monarchy.
It ended the war with Austria.
quiz.explanation: The law concentrated the Terror’s machinery in the Committee, and many feared Robespierre would use it against his opponents.

quiz.question: What mainly motivated the deputies who overthrew Robespierre in July 1794?
options: A plan to restore Louis XVI’s family to the throne.
Orders from the Austrian emperor.
A wish to make Robespierre king.
Saving themselves from the Terror.
quiz.explanation: The coup leaders acted to protect themselves; dismantling the Terror’s institutions took several more months.

quiz.question: A historian argues that war, regional revolts, and economic hardship drove France into the Terror. Which interpretation is this?
options: The Revolution was swept off course by circumstances.
The Terror was the unavoidable product of 1789’s principles.
The Terror never really happened.
The Terror was organized by foreign kings.
quiz.explanation: One school sees the Terror as unconnected to 1789 and caused by the crises of the moment; the other links it to the Revolution’s own principles.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the scale of the Terror according to Britannica?
options: Only the king and queen were executed.
About 300,000 people were executed in Paris alone.
About 17,000 people were tried and executed, and up to 23,000 more died without trial or in prison.
No one was executed outside Paris.
quiz.explanation: About 300,000 were arrested; 17,000 were tried and executed; as many as 23,000 more were killed without trial or died in prison.

quiz.question: Why did the Convention hand power to a twelve-member committee in 1793?
options: The king appointed the committee before his execution.
A divided legislature of some 600 members found it nearly impossible to govern in wartime.
The constitution required a committee in every republic.
The sans-culottes had abolished the Convention.
quiz.explanation: Faced with war and revolt, the faction-ridden Convention delegated power to the Committee of Public Safety.

topics.title: Genghis Khan
topics.summary: Genghis Khan united the Mongolian steppe in 1206 and launched conquests that laid the foundations of an enormous Eurasian empire, combining exceptional military organization with devastating violence.

lessons.title: Genghis Khan: Unification, Conquest, and Legacy

sections.heading: From Temüjin to Genghis Khan
sections.body:
Genghis Khan was born Temüjin, probably around 1162, although sources disagree about his birth year. He grew up among the pastoral nomadic peoples of the Mongolian steppe, where herding, alliances, and competition among groups shaped political life.

After hardship in his early life, Temüjin built alliances and defeated rivals, using both personal relationships and force to gather followers. He redistributed members of conquered or allied groups among his own units, reducing the influence of older tribal loyalties and directing allegiance toward himself.

In 1206, an assembly recognized him as ruler, and he took the title Genghis Khan, also written Chinggis Khan. Unifying the steppe mattered because it brought formerly competing groups under a single political and military leadership capable of launching coordinated campaigns beyond Mongolia.

sections.heading: Organization mattered as much as force
sections.body:
Genghis Khan organized his forces using a decimal structure, with units based on ten, one hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand. Personal loyalty between major commanders and the ruler helped hold these forces together and sustain his authority.

Mongol soldiers were skilled horsemen and archers, combining mobility with the ability to attack while mounted. Riders could change horses during long journeys, helping their armies maintain speed and surprise across large distances.

One important tactic was the feigned withdrawal: soldiers pretended to retreat, encouraging enemies to pursue them into a trap. Mongol success also involved adapting to opponents and learning siege techniques, showing that their armies were more than groups of riders relying on speed alone.

sections.heading: Conquest carried a devastating human cost
sections.body:
Genghis Khan's campaigns targeted states in northwestern and northern China, including the Xia and Jin, and later the Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia. Trade disputes and attacks on Mongol diplomatic representatives contributed to these conflicts, although their outcomes involved much more than adjustments to trade.

The invasion of Central Asia began in 1219 and brought devastating attacks on major urban centers, including Bukhara and Samarkand. Cities were destroyed, civilians were killed, and damage to irrigation systems harmed the conditions needed for settled life and agriculture.

Mongol forces used the threat of destruction to pressure other cities into surrender, making terror part of their strategy rather than simply an accidental consequence of fighting. A balanced assessment therefore needs to recognize military effectiveness without treating successful conquest as justification for massacres or the destruction of communities.

sections.heading: His empire continued to grow after his death
sections.body:
Genghis Khan also pursued measures to govern conquered territories, including adopting a writing system for Mongolian and allowing rulers in some regions to remain as subordinate authorities. His administration accommodated different religions and encouraged trade, but those policies coexisted with the brutality of conquest rather than canceling it out.

He died in 1227, and his son Ögödei became Great Khan in 1229, overseeing further major expansion. Later descendants extended Mongol rule still farther; his grandson Kublai completed the conquest of the Southern Song in China in 1279, decades after Genghis Khan's death.

The Mongol Empire ultimately became the largest contiguous land empire in world history, meaning its territories formed a connected landmass rather than primarily an overseas network. Genghis Khan founded that imperial project, but its full extent and its wider influence on Eurasian exchange resulted from developments under several generations of rulers.

keyFacts: Genghis Khan was born Temüjin; his birth year is uncertain, often given as about 1162.
He became ruler of the united Mongolian steppe in 1206.
Military units were based on ten, one hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand.
Mounted archery, mobility, and feigned retreats were important advantages.
His Central Asian campaigns devastated cities and killed civilians.
He died in 1227, and his successors substantially expanded the empire.

quiz.question: What was Genghis Khan's original name?
options: Osman.
Kublai.
Temüjin.
Süleyman.
quiz.explanation: Temüjin was his birth name; Genghis Khan was a title adopted after his rise to power.

quiz.question: Why was the year 1206 a turning point?
options: He completed the conquest of the Southern Song.
An assembly recognized his rule over the united Mongolian steppe.
The Ottoman sultanate was abolished.
He died and Ögödei immediately took the throne.
quiz.explanation: The assembly recognized his leadership in 1206, marking the establishment of his rule as Genghis Khan.

quiz.question: Which feature best describes the organization of his military forces?
options: Units based on ten, one hundred, one thousand, and ten thousand.
Every soldier acted independently without commanders.
Units were organized solely by the city where each soldier was born.
Only one permanent unit was permitted.
quiz.explanation: His military organization used a decimal structure.

quiz.question: A Mongol force appears to flee, lures an enemy into pursuit, and then attacks with waiting troops. What tactic is this?
options: A naval blockade.
A diplomatic surrender.
A siege conducted entirely from a fixed position.
A feigned withdrawal.
quiz.explanation: The apparent retreat is a deliberate maneuver intended to draw an enemy into a trap.

quiz.question: Which statement best evaluates the relationship between Mongol administrative policies and military violence?
options: Encouraging trade proves that no civilians were harmed.
Religious accommodation meant that conquest was always peaceful.
Administrative innovation and religious accommodation coexisted with destructive campaigns and massacres.
The existence of massacres means there were no governing institutions.
quiz.explanation: Governing innovations and accommodation do not erase the documented brutality of Mongol conquest.

quiz.question: Why is it inaccurate to credit Genghis Khan personally with every Mongol conquest?
options: He never led military campaigns.
His successors expanded the empire after his death in 1227.
The Mongol Empire ended before he became ruler.

title: Philosophy
description: Thinkers and schools that asked how we should live and what we can know.

topics.title: Socrates
topics.summary: The Athenian philosopher who taught by questioning and was put to death for it.

lessons.title: Socrates and the Examined Life

sections.heading: A philosopher who left no books
sections.body:
Socrates, who lived from 469 to 399 BCE, shaped Western philosophy so deeply that it is hard to imagine its history without him. Here is the surprise: he never wrote anything down. He spent his days in the agora, the Athenian marketplace, asking questions of anyone who would talk with him. Everything we know about his ideas comes from people who knew him or wrote about him.

Those sources do not agree. The comic playwright Aristophanes mocked him in Clouds (423 BCE) as a dangerous intellectual who could corrupt the whole city. Xenophon, who knew him, stresses his self-mastery and moderation. Plato, his most famous follower, made him the main speaker in many dialogues and remains our principal source. Working out which portrait is accurate is called the Socratic problem, and some scholars think finding the “real” Socrates is impossible.

So let one scene from Plato carry you through this lesson. In 399 BCE Socrates, then about seventy, walks to the stoa of the king archon, an Athenian official, for a preliminary hearing on a charge brought by a young poet named Meletus. On the way he falls into conversation with Euthyphro, a diviner he knows, about what piety, or reverence, really is. Plato’s dialogue Euthyphro records that conversation, and it shows you Socrates’ method, his mission, and the danger he was in.

sections.heading: Asking “What is it?”
sections.body:
Socrates typically opened with a deceptively simple question: what is it? What is courage, what is justice, what is piety? In Plato’s dialogue, Euthyphro offers five separate answers. Piety is prosecuting whoever does wrong. Piety is what the gods love. Piety is what all the gods love. Piety is the part of justice concerned with caring for the gods. Piety is knowing how to sacrifice and pray. Socrates tests and refutes each one.

This kind of cross-examination is called the elenchus. Socrates takes what someone says, asks further questions, and shows that the answer clashes with other things the person believes. Scholars disagree about what the elenchus can actually prove. If it only reveals that someone’s beliefs are inconsistent, how can Socrates conclude that a particular claim is false? Some argue it can establish positive results; others think its job is to expose confusion and improve the person being questioned.

Why spend his life this way? In Plato’s Apology, Socrates explains that his friend Chaerephon asked the oracle at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and was told no one was. Puzzled, Socrates questioned politicians, poets, and craftsmen, and found that each believed he knew more than he did. Socrates concluded he was better off only because he was aware of his own ignorance. Notice that this is not a claim to know nothing; he held firm convictions, such as that it is never just to harm anyone, while admitting he could not fully explain them.

sections.heading: On trial for impiety
sections.body:
The formal charge, as later reported by Diogenes Laertius, was that Socrates did not recognize the gods the city recognized, introduced new divinities, and corrupted the young. Socrates said he heard an inner sign or voice, his daimonion, that warned him away from certain actions, and it seems to have fed the charge about new gods. Here is the irony: Athens had no legal definition of piety. The jurors were in the same position as Euthyphro, needing to know what piety is before judging anyone guilty of lacking it.

Religion was not the whole story, and this part is a matter of interpretation. Athens had just endured the long Peloponnesian War against Sparta (431–404 BCE), and several of Socrates’ associates, including Alcibiades, were seen as sympathetic to Sparta or as traitors. Many Athenians viewed Socrates as a threat to their democracy, and that suspicion contributed to his conviction. Because of an amnesty after the war, the charges themselves were framed in religious terms.

Socrates was convicted and sentenced to death. In Plato’s Apology he tells the jury that he could never keep silent, because “the unexamined life is not worth living for human beings.” He compares himself to a gadfly stinging a sluggish horse, a city that needs to be roused to examine itself. He died after drinking hemlock. The conversation with Euthyphro never reached a definition of piety, but that was never quite the point: it showed how much people claim to know without having examined it.

keyFacts: Socrates lived from 469 to 399 BCE and wrote nothing himself.
Our main sources are Aristophanes, Xenophon, and above all Plato.
The elenchus is Socrates’ method of cross-examining a claim and refuting it.
He was charged with not recognizing the city’s gods, introducing new divinities, and corrupting the young.
In Plato’s Apology he says the unexamined life is not worth living.

quiz.question: A friend confidently defines courage. You ask a few more questions and show that the definition contradicts other things your friend believes. What method are you using?
options: The elenchus.
Stoic indifference.
The Socratic problem.
Divination.
quiz.explanation: The elenchus tests what someone says through cross-examination and refutes it, often by exposing inconsistency.

quiz.question: A historian notices that Aristophanes, Xenophon, and Plato give conflicting portraits of Socrates. What name do scholars give this difficulty?
options: The Euthyphro dilemma.
The Socratic problem.
Double ignorance.
The amnesty problem.
quiz.explanation: Because Socrates wrote nothing and the sources disagree, reconstructing the real Socrates is known as the Socratic problem.

quiz.question: In Plato’s Euthyphro, what happens to Euthyphro’s definitions of piety?
options: Socrates accepts the first one.
They consult the oracle to decide.
Socrates tests and refutes each one.
Euthyphro persuades Socrates to drop the question.
quiz.explanation: Euthyphro offers five definitions, and Socrates refutes each in turn without reaching a final answer.

quiz.question: Socrates concluded that he was wiser than the craftsmen he questioned. Why?
options: He knew more about their crafts than they did.
The oracle gave him secret knowledge.
He had written more books than they had.
He was aware of his own ignorance, while they believed they knew more than they did.
quiz.explanation: Socratic wisdom is awareness of one’s own lack of knowledge, in contrast to people who think they know what they do not.

quiz.question: A juror in 399 BCE must decide whether Socrates is impious, but Athens has no legal definition of piety. How does this situation echo the Euthyphro?
options: Like Euthyphro, the jurors need to know what piety is before they can judge it.
It shows that piety was precisely defined in Athenian law.
It means the trial was about taxes, not religion.
It proves Socrates wrote the law himself.
quiz.explanation: Without a legal definition, the jurors faced the same question Socrates pressed on Euthyphro: what is piety?

quiz.question: Why does Socrates call himself a gadfly in Plato’s Apology?
options: He wanted to escape Athens.
He believed the city, like a sluggish horse, needed to be stirred into examining itself.
He was mocking Aristophanes’ play.
He was asking the jury for a lighter penalty.
quiz.explanation: A gadfly irritates a horse but rouses it to action; Socrates saw his questioning as rousing Athens to self-examination.

topics.title: Stoicism
topics.summary: A school of philosophy, born in Athens and popular in Rome, that teaches virtue and calm acceptance of what we cannot control.

lessons.title: The Origins of Stoicism

sections.heading: A school named after a porch
sections.body:
Zeno was born around 335 BCE in Citium, on Cyprus, and went to Athens around 312 BCE. There he attended lectures by the Cynic philosopher Crates of Thebes and by Stilpon of Megara, as well as lectures at Plato’s Academy. He was also a voracious reader of the Socratic dialogues. Out of all of that he built his own philosophy.

Around 300 BCE Zeno began teaching in the Stoa Poikile, the “painted porch” or Painted Colonnade, a public space in Athens. The school took its name from the place: Stoics were the people of the stoa. It competed with the school Epicurus had founded in Athens shortly before. After Zeno, the school was led by Cleanthes of Assos and then by Chrysippus of Soli, who headed it from about 230 to 206 BCE and was its foremost theorist and systematizer.

One caution before going further. Not a single complete work by Zeno, Cleanthes, or Chrysippus survives. Chrysippus is reported to have written more than 150 works, and only fragments remain, so what we know of early Stoicism comes largely from later reports. To test the ideas, keep one situation in mind (a modern teaching example, not an ancient one): you have trained for months for a race, and on the morning of it you sprain your ankle and cannot run.

sections.heading: The only thing that is truly good
sections.body:
The Stoics divided philosophy into logic, physics, and ethics and insisted the parts fit together. They compared philosophy to an egg, with logic as the shell, ethics next, and physics innermost, or to a fertile field, where logic is the surrounding wall, physics the land and trees, and ethics the fruit. The point of the comparisons is that the goal of the whole system is ethical: becoming virtuous and living well.

Their most startling claim was that virtue is the only good. The virtues, such as prudence, justice, courage, and moderation, are good, and their opposites are bad. Everything else, including life, health, pleasure, beauty, strength, wealth, and reputation, is neither good nor bad. The Stoics called these things “indifferent,” because something truly good always benefits you, while wealth and health can harm as easily as they help. Apply that to your ankle: losing the race has not made you a worse person, and your character is still entirely yours.

“Indifferent” does not mean worthless, though. Health and wealth belong to a “preferred” type of indifferent: they have value, and a sensible person generally pursues them. So a Stoic with a sprained ankle still ices it, sees a doctor, and trains for the next race. What changes is how much rides on the outcome. The Stoic goal of life was summed up as “living in agreement with nature,” and for a rational creature that means letting reason, not fortune, steer.

sections.heading: Emotions as judgments, and an objection
sections.body:
The Stoics defined a passion as an impulse that is excessive and disobedient to reason. They also thought each passion follows an act of assent, so it can be analyzed as a judgment. In the standard case that judgment makes two mistakes: it gives something the wrong value, treating it as genuinely good or bad, and it decides that a particular reaction is called for. Picture the thought “This is a disaster and I should give up running.” A Stoic would ask you to examine both parts of it.

That is why the Stoics could make two of their most controversial claims: that happiness is fully in our power, and that the virtuous person feels no passions at all. If virtue is a kind of knowledge, and knowledge depends on what we assent to, then virtue, and with it happiness, is up to us. Notice how demanding this is. It is not advice to hide your feelings but a claim that, rightly understood, the injury never gave you a reason for despair.

Not everyone was convinced, and the disagreement is still debated. Philosophers in Plato’s Academy and Aristotle’s school objected that a terminally ill patient, wracked with pain, impoverished, and despised by everyone, cannot be happy even if virtuous. For them, virtue is necessary for happiness but not enough on its own. The Stoics rejected that view. Your ankle makes the Stoic answer easy to accept; the terminal illness case makes it much harder. Where you land is a good test of how far you would follow Zeno.

keyFacts: Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school in Athens around 300 BCE.
The name comes from the Stoa Poikile, the painted porch where Zeno taught.
Cleanthes and then Chrysippus led the school after Zeno; no complete work by any of the three survives.
The Stoics held that virtue is the only good, and that health and wealth are “indifferents.”
The Stoic goal of life was “living in agreement with nature.”

quiz.question: An early Stoic loses her savings in a market crash. How would early Stoic ethics classify wealth?
options: As the highest good.
As something evil that must be avoided.
As an indifferent: neither good nor bad in itself.
As a virtue, like courage.
quiz.explanation: The Stoics counted wealth among the indifferents, which can harm as easily as they benefit.

quiz.question: Should that Stoic try to rebuild her savings?
options: Yes, because wealth is a preferred indifferent with value, even though it is not truly good.
No, because indifferents are completely worthless.
Yes, because wealth is the only good.
No, because the Stoics required everyone to live in poverty.
quiz.explanation: Preferred indifferents such as health and wealth have value, and a sensible person generally pursues them.

quiz.question: You feel a surge of panic: “This is a catastrophe, and I have to run away.” What would a Stoic analysis say about this reaction?
options: It is a bodily reflex with no connection to judgment.
It is the correct response to a true evil.
It proves that happiness is outside our control.
It rests on judgments that give the situation the wrong value and call for the wrong response.
quiz.explanation: The Stoics analyzed passions as judgments that typically misjudge value and what reaction is appropriate.

quiz.question: A student reads a confident modern summary of Chrysippus’ views. Why should she treat it with some caution?
options: Chrysippus wrote only one short book.
None of his works survives complete; we rely on fragments and later reports.
Chrysippus was not a Stoic.
His works were written after Marcus Aurelius.
quiz.explanation: Chrysippus reportedly wrote over 150 works, but only fragments remain.

quiz.question: A Stoic compares philosophy to a fertile field. What does the fruit stand for?
options: Ethics.
Logic.
Physics.
Rhetoric.
quiz.explanation: In the field comparison, logic is the wall, physics the land and trees, and ethics the fruit: the goal of the whole system.

quiz.question: A critic says, “A virtuous person who is dying in pain, poor, and despised cannot be happy.” Where does this view come from?
options: It is the official Stoic position.
It comes from Zeno’s teacher Crates.
It is the Academic and Peripatetic objection, which the Stoics rejected.
It is a modern idea with no ancient parallel.
quiz.explanation: Academic and Peripatetic philosophers argued that virtue is necessary but not sufficient for happiness; the Stoics rejected this.

lessons.title: The Roman Stoics

sections.heading: Seneca: philosophy close to power
sections.body:
Stoicism became especially fashionable in the Roman period. The only complete works by Stoic philosophers that survive come from this imperial era, above all from Seneca, Epictetus, and Marcus Aurelius. Follow one thread through all three: the Roman imperial court. Seneca advised an emperor, Epictetus was enslaved to a man who had served one, and Marcus Aurelius was emperor himself.

Seneca was born around 1 BCE in Corduba, in Spain. Exiled by the emperor Claudius, he was recalled in 49 CE with the help of Agrippina, Claudius’s wife, and became tutor to her son, the young Nero. When Nero took power in 54 CE, Seneca was among his advisers. His most widely read work, the Moral Letters to Lucilius, survives as 124 letters in 20 books. In his writings he attacks the ideas that wealth is a good, that death is an evil, and that anger is justified.

The story ends badly. As Nero matured he relied less on Seneca, and Seneca was eventually named as an associate in the failed Pisonian conspiracy to overthrow him. In 65 CE Nero ordered him to take his own life. His reputation is still debated. Seneca wrote that poverty is no evil while being one of the wealthiest men in the world, and critics since antiquity have called him a hypocrite. Some scholars, notably Emily Wilson, ask a different question: why he preached what he did so forcefully, given the life he led.

sections.heading: Epictetus: what is up to us
sections.body:
Epictetus was born in the 50s CE in Hierapolis, a Greek city in Asia Minor. He spent part of his life enslaved to Epaphroditus, a rich and powerful freedman who had himself been enslaved to Nero and had served as an administrator in Nero’s court. That is the court thread again. Epictetus studied with the Stoic Musonius Rufus, was eventually freed, and began teaching. When the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from Rome (the sources differ on the year), he left and founded a school at Nicopolis in north-western Greece.

What we know of his teaching comes through his student Arrian, who recorded it in the Discourses and in a short abridgment called the Encheiridion, or Handbook. Its central idea is a sorting exercise: some things are “in our power” or “up to us,” and some are not. What is up to us is our capacity to judge what is good and bad, our moral character. Health, wealth, status, and how events turn out are “external things,” not fully in our control.

His own example makes it concrete. Sickness is not in our power, since it is not wholly up to us whether we get sick or recover. It makes sense to see a doctor, but the doctor’s skill and whether the treatment works are not up to us either. What is up to us is how we judge what happens and how we respond to it. Coming from someone who had been enslaved, the claim that no one else is master of your moral character carried real weight.

sections.heading: Marcus Aurelius: notes to himself
sections.body:
Marcus Aurelius was born in 121 CE and became emperor in 161, at first ruling alongside Lucius Verus and alone from 169, until his death in 180. His reign was troubled by attacks from Germany, rebellions in northern Italy and Egypt, and an outbreak of plague. He spent much of it on military campaigns in central Europe, and that is where the work he is famous for was likely written.

The Meditations is a personal notebook, probably written on campaign around 171–175 CE. Its entries appear in no particular order, and it was not a treatise meant to argue a doctrine for readers; Marcus wrote it to himself and for his own use. Even its Greek title, usually translated “To Himself,” comes from a manuscript now lost and may have been added later.

Here the court thread closes. In the Meditations Marcus records borrowing a copy of the works of Epictetus, and Epictetus’s teachings, as recorded by Arrian, deeply influenced him. The most powerful man in the Roman world was learning from a former slave. One nuance: nowhere in the Meditations does Marcus call himself a Stoic. That may simply be because he was writing for himself rather than presenting himself to an audience.

quiz.question: You get sick, see an excellent doctor, and the treatment still fails. According to Epictetus, what was up to you?
options: Whether you got sick.
How well the doctor did the job.
How you judged and responded to what happened.
Whether the treatment worked.
quiz.explanation: For Epictetus, illness, the doctor’s skill, and the outcome are not in our power; our judgments and responses are.

quiz.question: A critic says Seneca’s praise of poverty cannot be taken seriously. What is the criticism based on?
options: He was one of the wealthiest men in the world while writing that poverty is no evil.
He never wrote about poverty.
He refused to advise Nero.
He lived his whole life in exile.
quiz.explanation: Critics since antiquity have contrasted Seneca’s enormous wealth with his teaching that poverty is not an evil.

quiz.question: A student wants to read Epictetus in his own words. What should she understand about the texts?
options: Epictetus wrote the Meditations.
His teaching survives only in a few lines quoted by Seneca.
He wrote everything in Latin poetry.
His teaching comes to us through the Discourses and Handbook recorded by his student Arrian.
quiz.explanation: Our knowledge of Epictetus comes through two works composed by his student Arrian.

quiz.question: Expecting a carefully organized argument, a reader finds the Meditations full of short, unordered entries. Why?
options: It was a personal notebook Marcus wrote to himself, probably on campaign.
It was assembled by Seneca from Marcus’s speeches.
It was a textbook for Stoic students.
Later editors scrambled a single long treatise.
quiz.explanation: The Meditations takes the form of a personal notebook written for Marcus’s own use, not a treatise for readers.

quiz.question: What connects Epictetus to the court of Nero?
options: He was Nero’s tutor.
He was enslaved to Epaphroditus, a freedman who had served as an administrator in Nero’s court.
He led the Pisonian conspiracy.
He was Nero’s brother.
quiz.explanation: Epaphroditus had been enslaved to Nero and worked in his court before becoming Epictetus’s owner.

quiz.question: Which fact best shows Epictetus’s influence on Marcus Aurelius?
options: Epictetus served as Marcus’s chief minister.
Marcus called himself a Stoic in every entry.
Marcus records borrowing a copy of Epictetus’s works, whose teachings deeply influenced him.
Epictetus wrote the Meditations for Marcus.
quiz.explanation: Marcus mentions borrowing Epictetus’s works, and Epictetus’s recorded teachings heavily influenced him.

title: Ancient History
description: The earliest civilizations, the laws they wrote, and what their records reveal.

topics.title: The Code of Hammurabi
topics.summary: The Code of Hammurabi is an ancient Babylonian collection of legal decisions that reveals how a society organized everyday life, punishment, and social hierarchy.

lessons.title: What Ancient Laws Tell Us About Everyday Life

sections.heading: A king puts justice on display
sections.body:
Imagine trying to understand a civilization without meeting anyone who lived there. Where would you begin? Its laws offer one useful starting point. They reveal what people owned, what they argued about, and which behaviors authorities wanted to punish. The Code of Hammurabi gives us this kind of window into ancient Babylon, through rules concerning everything from business transactions to family relationships.

Hammurabi ruled Babylon from approximately 1792 to 1750 BCE. Toward the end of his reign, legal decisions were collected and inscribed on a stone monument called a stele. The collection is conventionally described as containing 282 case laws. It connected the king's authority with the administration of justice and presented legal decisions in a durable, visible form.

A surviving stele was discovered at Susa in 1901 and is now preserved in the Louvre in Paris. Its survival lets historians examine the collection directly rather than relying only on later descriptions. But a monument is not a complete record of everyday court proceedings. To understand its significance, we need to distinguish the rules it presents from everything that actually happened in Babylonian life.

sections.heading: Laws about more than crime
sections.body:
When you hear “ancient law,” you might picture dramatic punishments. But much of Hammurabi's collection concerns ordinary practical problems: trade, prices, debt, marriage, divorce, and property. These subjects reveal a society in which households, workers, merchants, and landowners had complicated relationships. Law was not just about catching criminals; it also concerned organizing obligations between people.

Many provisions take the form of cases: if a particular situation occurs, a particular consequence follows. That approach differs from beginning with a broad declaration of individual rights. The collection addresses specific disputes and responsibilities, including damage to fields and crops. Its concrete details make it especially valuable for understanding the kinds of problems authorities considered worth addressing.

Imagine a disagreement over livestock damaging someone else's crops. The underlying questions remain recognizable: Who caused the damage? Who should bear the loss? What compensation or penalty is appropriate? This is a modern teaching example, not a quotation from the code. It illustrates why ancient legal collections can feel surprisingly familiar even when their solutions differ greatly from ours.

sections.heading: Order did not mean equality
sections.body:
The code's punishments could be extremely severe. It is associated with the principle of retaliation, often summarized as “an eye for an eye.” Under this approach, a punishment could mirror an injury. But that phrase does not explain the entire collection: its provisions also addressed economic transactions, family obligations, and other matters that had nothing to do with bodily punishment.

Social status mattered. Penalties varied according to people's status and the circumstances of an offense. Enslavement was part of the society the laws regulated, not a practice they abolished. We should therefore avoid confusing an organized legal system with equal justice. Rules can make relationships more predictable while still preserving deep inequalities between groups.

Nor was the collection an exhaustive answer to every possible dispute. Its cases covered many everyday situations without attempting to address all contingencies. Read it as both a legal collection and historical evidence: it shows what rulers sought to regulate, which distinctions mattered, and how power shaped punishment. Its lasting importance lies in the questions it lets us ask about ancient society.

quiz.explanation: Penalties depended partly on status, rather than treating everyone equally.

options: That it gives a complete record of every dispute and how it was handled.

quiz.explanation: The collection did not attempt to cover every possible contingency.

title: American Civics
description: How the U.S. Constitution organizes government and protects individual rights.

topics.title: The Constitutional Convention of 1787
topics.summary: The Constitutional Convention created a new framework for American government by strengthening national authority while dividing power among institutions and making consequential compromises over representation and slavery.

lessons.title: How the Constitution Divided Power

sections.heading: Why the country needed a new framework
sections.body:
Before the Constitution, the United States operated under the Articles of Confederation, a framework that left the states largely independent. The national government had responsibilities such as common defense, but it could not levy taxes or regulate trade between the states, leaving it without important tools for carrying out those responsibilities.

This weakness created a practical problem: national responsibilities required resources that the government could not reliably obtain. Disputes among the states over trade, taxation, territory, and war pensions also threatened the country's unity.

Delegates gathered in Philadelphia in 1787 with instructions to revise the Articles, but they instead developed an entirely new Constitution. Their challenge was to create a government strong enough to handle national problems without concentrating too much power in one place.

sections.heading: Dividing power in two different ways
sections.body:
The Constitution divided national authority among three branches, an arrangement called separation of powers. In a useful introductory shorthand, Congress makes laws, the executive branch led by the president enforces laws, and the judicial branch interprets laws.

The branches were not designed to operate in complete isolation: checks and balances give them ways to limit one another's actions. For example, the president can veto legislation, but Congress can override that veto with a two-thirds vote in each house.

The Constitution also divided authority between the national government and the states, a system called federalism. Keep the distinction clear: separation of powers concerns different branches of government, while federalism concerns different levels of government.

sections.heading: Representation, compromise, and slavery
sections.body:
Large and small states disagreed about how representation in Congress should work: populous states generally favored representation based on population, while smaller states sought an equal voice for each state. The Great Compromise combined the two approaches by basing House representation on population and giving every state two senators.

Slavery exposed a deeper injustice within the debate over representation. Under the Three-Fifths Compromise, three-fifths of a state's enslaved population counted when allocating House seats and direct taxes among the states. The formula concerned population accounting for political representation and taxation, not a grant of three-fifths of the rights of citizenship.

The agreement accommodated slavery rather than abolishing it: the Constitution also protected the international slave trade from congressional prohibition until 1808 and required the return of people who escaped enslavement across state lines. Understanding the Convention therefore requires recognizing both its institutional innovations and the protections it gave to an oppressive system.

sections.heading: A proposal still needed public approval
sections.body:
Signing the Constitution on September 17, 1787, did not by itself put the new government into operation. The document had to be ratified, meaning formally approved, through special conventions in the states, with approval from nine of the thirteen states required under its ratification rule.

Supporters, known as Federalists, argued that a stronger national government was necessary to address the country's problems. Opponents, known as Anti-Federalists, feared excessive central power and objected that the proposed Constitution lacked a bill of rights.

Promises to add a bill of rights helped the Constitution gain approval, and James Madison later led the effort to draft those amendments in the First Congress. This final debate highlighted two different approaches to protecting liberty: organizing government so that power checks power, and expressly identifying rights that government must respect.

keyFacts: Convention: Delegates met in Philadelphia in 1787 to revise the Articles but wrote a new Constitution instead.
Separation of powers: National authority is divided among legislative, executive, and judicial branches.
Federalism: Authority is divided between the national government and the states.
Great Compromise: House representation follows population; each state has two senators.
Three-Fifths Compromise: Three-fifths of the enslaved population counted for allocating House representation and direct taxes.
Ratification: Approval from nine states was required, and the lack of a bill of rights became a major objection.

quiz.question: What was a major weakness of the national government under the Articles of Confederation?
options: It could levy taxes without any legal limits.
It could not levy taxes to fund its responsibilities.
It gave the president authority to dissolve Congress.
It prohibited states from running their own governments.
quiz.explanation: The national government lacked the power to tax.

quiz.question: Which arrangement illustrates separation of powers rather than federalism?
options: Dividing authority between state and national governments.
Allowing different states to have different policies.
Dividing national authority among Congress, the president, and the courts.
Giving every state two senators.
quiz.explanation: Separation of powers divides authority among branches, not between national and state governments.

quiz.question: A president vetoes a bill, and Congress then overrides the veto with the required votes. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Checks and balances.
Government by a single branch.
Equal representation of states.
Ratification by state conventions.
quiz.explanation: A presidential veto and congressional override allow the branches to check one another.

quiz.question: What arrangement resulted from the Great Compromise?
options: Equal state representation in both houses of Congress.
Population-based representation in both houses of Congress.
One house of Congress with one vote per state.
Population-based House representation and equal state representation in the Senate.
quiz.explanation: The compromise combined population-based representation in the House with two senators per state.

quiz.question: What did the Three-Fifths Compromise determine?
options: The proportion of enslaved people who would immediately be freed.
How the enslaved population counted for allocating House seats and direct taxes.
The proportion of enslaved people allowed to vote.
The share of Senate seats reserved for slaveholding states.
quiz.explanation: The formula applied to representation and direct taxation, not emancipation or voting rights.

quiz.question: Why did promises to add a bill of rights help the Constitution win approval?
options: They guaranteed every state the same population.
They eliminated the national government's taxing power.
They addressed concerns that the new government lacked explicit protections for individual liberties.
They replaced state ratifying conventions with a presidential decision.
quiz.explanation: The absence of a bill of rights was a serious objection during ratification, and promises to add one helped secure support.

topics.title: The Adoption of the Bill of Rights
topics.summary: Ratified in 1791, the Bill of Rights added ten amendments to the U.S. Constitution to protect liberties and place explicit limits on government power.

lessons.title: Why the Constitution Needed a Bill of Rights

sections.heading: A strong government raised a difficult question
sections.body:
Imagine helping create a new government. You want it strong enough to address national problems, but you also worry about what it might do with that power. How do you keep strength from becoming abuse? This was a central concern in the debate over the U.S. Constitution. A framework explaining how government operates did not satisfy everyone who wanted explicit protections for liberty.

The Constitution signed in 1787 did not contain a separate bill of rights. Critics feared that the new national government could threaten individual freedoms, and the absence of explicit protections became an important objection during ratification. Supporters argued that the Constitution's structure already restrained power. Promises to add amendments helped address the disagreement and build support for the new system.

James Madison helped advance those amendments in Congress. In 1789, Congress proposed twelve; ten received the necessary state approval by December 15, 1791. Those ten became the Bill of Rights. This distinction matters: the amendments were not part of the original signed Constitution, but additions adopted through its amendment process.

sections.heading: Protecting expression and private life
sections.body:
The First Amendment protects freedom of religion, speech, and the press, along with peaceful assembly and petitioning the government. These protections concern more than speaking freely in conversation. They address ways people practice beliefs, circulate information, gather with others, and ask officials to correct problems. The amendment's wording places restrictions on government rather than simply praising these activities as desirable.

Religious liberty has two parts in the First Amendment: government may not establish religion, and it may not prohibit its free exercise. Keep those ideas distinct. One addresses government's relationship with religious institutions; the other protects religious practice. Both appear in the same sentence because freedom of religion involves more than a single kind of protection.

Other amendments address different concerns. The Third restricts quartering soldiers in private homes. The Fourth protects against unreasonable searches and seizures and sets requirements for warrants, including probable cause and particular descriptions of the places and things involved. It does not prohibit every search. Its language draws attention to the conditions under which government may intrude.

sections.heading: Rights matter when someone is accused
sections.body:
Some protections become especially important when government accuses a person of a crime. The Fifth Amendment includes protections against compelled self-incrimination and being tried twice for the same offense, along with a guarantee of due process. These safeguards concern the way government exercises its power, not merely whether officials believe an accusation is correct.

The Sixth Amendment addresses criminal proceedings, including a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury, information about the accusation, and assistance of counsel. The Eighth prohibits excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments. Together, these provisions show that constitutional protection does not end when someone is accused or convicted: legal procedures and punishment also require limits.

Finally, the Ninth says that listing certain rights must not be understood to deny others retained by the people. The Tenth reserves powers not delegated to the United States, nor prohibited to the states, to the states or the people. The distinction is useful: one warns against treating a list of rights as exhaustive; the other concerns the allocation of government power.

keyFacts: The Bill of Rights consists of the first ten constitutional amendments.
Congress proposed twelve amendments in 1789; ten were ratified by December 15, 1791.
The First Amendment protects religion, expression, assembly, and petition.
The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
The Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth include safeguards concerning accusation, trials, and punishment.
The Ninth concerns unlisted rights; the Tenth concerns reserved powers.

quiz.question: What is the Bill of Rights?
options: The original Articles of Confederation.
The first ten amendments to the Constitution.
A list of presidential appointments.
The complete Constitution.
quiz.explanation: The Bill of Rights consists of the first ten constitutional amendments.

quiz.question: Why did promises to add a bill of rights help the Constitution win support?
options: They removed all national authority.
They abolished state governments.
They addressed fears about government power and insufficient protections for liberty.
They eliminated the amendment process.
quiz.explanation: Explicit protections responded to concerns raised during ratification.

quiz.question: Which activity is expressly protected by the First Amendment?
options: Quartering soldiers in private homes.
Conducting any search without justification.
Requiring a person to testify against themselves.
Peacefully assembling and petitioning the government.
quiz.explanation: Assembly and petition are among the First Amendment’s protections.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the Fourth Amendment?
options: It protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.
It prohibits every government search.
It concerns the number of senators.
It requires all trials to be secret.
quiz.explanation: The amendment restricts unreasonable searches and seizures and sets warrant requirements.

quiz.question: Which distinction between the Ninth and Tenth Amendments is correct?
options: Both list all rights that anyone can possess.
The Ninth concerns unlisted rights; the Tenth concerns reserved powers.
The Ninth regulates warrants; the Tenth regulates bail.
Both abolish state authority.
quiz.explanation: The Ninth addresses rights retained by the people; the Tenth addresses powers reserved to the states or the people.

title: Art History
description: Movements and makers that changed how people see and make pictures.

topics.title: The Italian Renaissance
topics.summary: The Italian Renaissance was a period of renewed interest in ancient Greek and Roman culture during which artists developed influential ways to depict people, emotion, and three-dimensional space.

lessons.title: How Renaissance Artists Made Pictures Feel Real

sections.heading: A rebirth, not a fresh start
sections.body:
Imagine looking at a painting and feeling that you could step inside it. The figures seem solid, the room stretches into the distance, and the faces suggest real emotions. During the Renaissance, artists explored ways to create these effects, transforming how they represented people and their surroundings. Their pictures were not simply windows onto reality, but carefully constructed illusions.

The word “Renaissance” means rebirth. It describes a period in European culture, roughly spanning the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries, associated with renewed interest in ancient Greece and Rome. In Italy, artists looked to classical art while studying the human body and the natural world. Looking backward became a way of developing something new.

This was not an overnight break with everything medieval. Earlier artists, including Giotto, had already explored solid-looking figures and expressive storytelling. Religious subjects also remained important during the Renaissance. What changed was often how those subjects appeared: sacred figures could occupy recognizable landscapes, show human emotions, and seem to inhabit the same physical world as the viewer.

sections.heading: Making a flat surface look deep
sections.body:
One of the Renaissance’s important artistic developments was linear perspective: a mathematical method for suggesting depth on a flat surface. In a simple one-point system, lines representing parallel edges receding directly away from the viewer appear to meet at a single vanishing point. That shared point helps make the painted space look coherent rather than arbitrary.

Think about standing in a long, straight hallway. Its walls do not actually move closer together, but their edges appear to converge in the distance. A painter can imitate that appearance. Floor tiles, ceilings, and rows of columns become useful guides, helping establish where objects belong and how large they should appear within the scene.

Other techniques strengthened the illusion. Foreshortening makes an object or body part appear shorter when it points toward or away from the viewer. Light and shadow can make a figure look rounded rather than flat. The early Renaissance painter Masaccio combined convincing light with careful perspective, producing figures that appear to have weight and occupy believable space.

sections.heading: People became worth a closer look
sections.body:
Renaissance art also reflected humanism, an outlook connected with renewed attention to classical culture and human life. Artists closely studied bodies, faces, and the surrounding world. This interest did not necessarily replace religious belief; it could change how religious stories were presented, making their figures more physically convincing and emotionally recognizable.

Portraiture offered another way to explore individuality. Artists in Florence, Venice, and Italian courts depicted rulers, church leaders, scholars, patrons, and others. A portrait could communicate recognizable appearance, personality, and social position. These were not simply pictures of interchangeable people: particular faces and identities became central to the work.

When you encounter a Renaissance painting, ask three questions: How does the artist suggest depth? What makes the bodies seem solid? What do the faces or gestures communicate? Do not expect every work to use the same formula. Paolo Uccello, for example, combined an interest in perspective with decorative features associated with Gothic art. Renaissance innovation could coexist with older traditions.

keyFacts: The Renaissance roughly spanned the fourteenth through sixteenth centuries.
Artists renewed their interest in ancient Greek and Roman culture.
Linear perspective uses geometry to create an illusion of depth.
Foreshortening suggests that an object extends toward or away from the viewer.
Masaccio combined perspective with light to create convincing figures in space.
Religious art remained important as portraiture and other subjects developed.

quiz.question: What does “Renaissance” mean?
options: Rebirth.
Royal rule.
Religious separation.
Perfect imitation.
quiz.explanation: The name refers to renewed interest in classical culture and learning.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of linear perspective?
options: To ensure every figure is the same size.
To remove architecture from paintings.
To create an illusion of three-dimensional space on a flat surface.
To replace all shadows with bright colors.
quiz.explanation: Linear perspective uses mathematical relationships to make painted space appear deep and coherent.

quiz.question: In a one-point perspective painting, the receding edges of a hallway appear to meet in the distance. What is that meeting place called?
options: The foreground.
The vanishing point.
The portrait plane.
The shadow line.
quiz.explanation: The vanishing point is where the relevant receding parallel lines appear to converge.

quiz.question: An artist paints an arm reaching toward the viewer so that it appears shorter than an arm seen from the side. Which technique is being used?
options: Portraiture.
Classical symbolism.
Decorative patterning.
Foreshortening.
quiz.explanation: Foreshortening changes the apparent length of a form to suggest its orientation in space.

quiz.question: Which statement best describes the relationship between Renaissance art and religious subjects?
options: Religious subjects disappeared from Renaissance painting.
Only portraits were considered important.
Religious subjects remained important, often depicted with more convincing bodies, settings, and emotions.
Renaissance artists were required to copy medieval paintings exactly.
quiz.explanation: New approaches to representation changed religious art rather than simply replacing it.

quiz.question: Why is it misleading to say that Renaissance artists abandoned every earlier artistic tradition?
options: Artists could combine newer techniques with older approaches.
No Renaissance painter used perspective.
Classical art had no influence on Renaissance artists.
All Renaissance paintings were identical to medieval paintings.
quiz.explanation: Uccello, for example, combined linear perspective with Gothic figure styles and decorative effects.
